exp.4:10:
The explanation says that, because of what God has already done for us, believers should encourage and strengthen one another. The word "comfort" means giving courage and consolation. "Edify" means helping one another grow in faith, the way a house is built up. The phrase "even as you do" shows that they were already practicing it.

Paul writes to the church in Thessalonica, which was going through trials and had doubts about believers who had died. Earlier he reminded them that God did not appoint them to wrath, but to salvation through Christ, who died for them. Therefore, whether we live or die, we will be with him. From that hope comes this mutual encouragement.

Today, think of someone in your church or family who is tired or sad. Write to them or call them this week, and encourage them with a sincere word based on the hope we have in Christ.
exp.2:8:
In what he says: Paul asks in wonder, "How can we thank God enough for you?" The word "thanks" here simply means "thanksgiving." Paul says he feels such joy over the Thessalonians that he cannot find words to thank God as fully as he would like. He lives this joy "before our God," that is, sincerely in God's presence.

Context: Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy to a young church that was under pressure. Timothy had just brought them good news: they remained firm in faith and love. After times of distress, Paul is filled with relief and joy. That is why he gives thanks to God and keeps praying to see them again.

For today: Think of someone whose faith or kindness has encouraged you. Thank God for that person and, if you can, tell them today with a sincere call or message.
exp.4:21:
It says we should stay away from evil in any of its forms. The word "kind" here means "sort" or "type." Some older translations understand it as "appearance," and the Greek term can carry both meanings. Either way, the idea is not to come near what harms.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, a young church. He has just asked them to test everything and hold fast to what is good. The opposite of holding fast to what is good is turning away from what is evil. Right after, he reminds them that God himself sanctifies them and is faithful to complete his work in them.

For today: before you view some content, accept a deal, or enter a conversation, ask yourself whether it brings you closer to or farther from what pleases God. If it pulls you away, step back calmly and ask God for the strength to do so.
exp.3:3:
It says that every believer must know how to control or care for his own body in a holy and honorable way. The word "vessel" is an image here; the explanation says it is an unusual word for this sense, and in this verse the image is the one rendered as "vessel." "You all" means the readers as a group, and "desire" in the sense of disordered longing is what is meant by the wrong kind of desire. Scholars read this in two ways: some understand "vessel" as the body itself, and others as one's own wife. Both readings call for purity and respect.

Paul writes to the Christians of Thessalonica, a young church made up of people who came from pagan customs. He reminds them of the instructions he had already given them in the name of Jesus. His point is that God wants them to live set apart for Him, especially in sexual matters, and not to treat others with abuse or deceit.

For today: before you act or give in to a desire, ask yourself whether what you are doing honors God and respects the other person. Ask the Lord for self-control and help to care for your body and your relationships with purity.
exp.2:3:
Paul reminds the Thessalonians that, when he was with them, he already warned them that they would suffer tribulations, that is, hardships and persecution. And that is exactly what happened, as they themselves know. The phrase "were to undergo" means that this was going to happen without fail.

Paul writes from a distance, concerned for the young church in Thessalonica, which was suffering opposition. For that reason he sent Timothy to strengthen them in the faith. He reminds them that the suffering did not catch them by surprise, since they had already been warned. In this way, they could understand that suffering did not mean that God had abandoned them or that the message was false.

For today: when trials come because you follow Christ, or simply because you live in this world, do not immediately think that God has forgotten you. Remember what He has already said, and seek the support of brothers and sisters in the faith who will encourage you to remain firm.
exp.3:11:
This verse says that believers should live in a worthy and respectable way before those who do not believe ("them that are without"). "Honestly" does not speak only of telling the truth, but of living with a good testimony, with propriety. And "have lack of nothing" means not depending on others to live.

Paul writes to the Christians of Thessalonica. He asks them to live quietly, attend to their responsibilities, and work with their hands. Some scholars think there were people who neglected their work, although the text gives no further details.

For today: work responsibly and keep your commitments. An orderly life, without scandal or abuse, speaks of God's love more than many speeches. And when you are able to support yourself, you will also be able to help others.
exp.1:18:
Paul asks: what is it that gives us the greatest joy and that we can be proud of? And he answers himself: you, the believers in Thessalonica. The word "or" introduces the alternatives, and his phrase about being proud carries the sense of boasting with gratitude. The reward of a winner is what it was pointing to, a crown given as a prize. All of this will happen in the presence of Jesus, at his coming, that is, when he returns.

Paul writes to a young church that he had to leave suddenly. He tells them that he misses them deeply and that he wanted to return several times, but something stood in the way, and he does not explain exactly what it was. His affection is that of a pastor who loves his people.

Today we can value the people God has placed along our path, such as family, friends, and the church. Encourage them, pray for them, and thank them. What lasts most is the life of those we love in Christ.
exp.0:0:
This verse is the greeting with which the letter begins. Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy write to the church of the Thessalonians, that is, to the believers in the city of Thessalonica. The verse says this church lives in God the Father and in the Lord Jesus Christ, meaning it is united with them. They wish the readers grace and peace: grace is the undeserved favor of God, and peace is well-being and tranquility that come from Him. The word "you" in the verse is addressed to the church itself.

Paul writes together with his travel companions, Silvanus (also called Silas) and Timothy, who had been with him in Thessalonica according to the book of Acts. They write to encourage a young church that was facing opposition. Many scholars think this is one of Paul's oldest letters, although the exact date is debated.

Today we can remember that our identity is "in God" and in Christ, not in our circumstances. When you face pressure, ask God for His grace and His peace, and wish the same for those around you.
exp.3:12:
Paul says that he does not want the believers to be without knowledge of what happens to "those who are asleep," that is, the Christians who have already died. "Be ignorant" means "not know," and "sorrow" refers to a grief without comfort. He does not forbid mourning, but asks that they not grieve as those who have no hope.

Paul writes to the church in Thessalonica, a young community facing pressure and doubts. Earlier he had spoken to them about living with order and honest work. Now he responds to their concern for the believers who died before the coming of the Lord. Speaking of the death of believers as "sleep" was a common way of referring to it among the first Christians.

When a loss comes, you can grieve sincerely and, at the same time, hold on to the promise that Jesus rose again. Share this hope with someone who is mourning.
exp.3:14:
The explanation says that Christians who are still alive when the Lord returns will have no advantage over those who have already died. The verse's word "prevent" means to go ahead of or get in front of someone, so the reader can see that the living will not get ahead of the dead. "Asleep" is a gentle way of speaking about believers who have died. Paul says he states this with the authority of the Lord, that is, with the authority of God.

Paul is writing to the believers in Thessalonica, who were sad and confused about the brothers and sisters who had died. They feared that those who had died would miss the return of Christ. Paul comforts them and assures them that the dead in Christ will rise first. Christians have understood the details of the last times in different ways, but the central comfort is clear.

When you suffer the loss of a believing loved one, weep, but not as someone who has no hope. Repeat this promise of God and comfort others with it.
exp.0:3:
Paul tells the believers in Thessalonica that he knows God loves them and has chosen them. The word "election" means that God called them and made them part of his people. "Knowing" means being sure of something.

Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy to a young church that was under pressure because of its faith. Before giving advice, he encourages them and thanks God for them. The verses that follow explain how that choosing was seen: the gospel came with power, they received it with joy, and they changed the way they lived. Christians have understood election in different ways, but here the emphasis is on encouragement and God's love.

For today: if you believe in Christ, rest in the fact that God loves you and called you. Let that assurance move you to serve with faith, love, and perseverance, even in difficult times.
exp.2:11:
Paul prays that the Lord will make the Thessalonians grow and fill them with love, both toward one another and toward all people. Paul's own affection for them is the example of this love.

Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy to a young church that was under pressure and rejection. He tells them that he prays night and day to see them again. While that time has not yet come, he asks God to make their love grow, so that their hearts will be firm and blameless when Christ comes.

Today we can ask God that our love not be limited to family or to the church. This week, do something concrete for someone who is hard for you to love: make a phone call, offer help, or pray sincerely for that person.
exp.2:7:
Paul says that now "we live," meaning he feels renewed life and encouragement, on the condition that the Thessalonians keep standing firm in the Lord. To stand firm means to remain faithful and not fall away.

Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy. They had been forced to leave Thessalonica because of persecution, and they were worried about those new believers. Timothy returned with good news of their faith and love. Paul had been living in distress, and hearing that they remained firm restored his spirit. When he says "we live," he is speaking of relief and joy, not mere survival.

Today we can encourage others by our steadfastness, because one person's faith strengthens many. We can also ask ourselves who needs our prayer, a phone call, or a message to learn how they are doing in their faith.
exp.2:4:
Paul says that he could no longer bear the worry about the Thessalonians. So he sent someone to find out how their faith was, that is, to learn how they were doing. He feared that the tempter, that is Satan, had caused them to fall, and that all his labor among them had been in vain, without fruit.

Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy to a young church that was suffering persecution. He had been forced to leave the city quickly, and he did not know how they were doing. According to the next verse, he sent Timothy, who came back with good news of their faith and love.

For today: do not assume that others are well in their faith. If someone is going through a trial, seek them out, ask how they are, encourage them, and pray for them. A timely message or visit can help them stay firm.
exp.1:9:
Paul says that the Thessalonians and God himself can bear witness to how he and his companions conducted themselves. Their behavior toward the believers was holy (set apart for God), just (honest and upright), and blameless (with nothing that could be held against them). "Ye" in the verse means "you," and "behaved ourselves" means "conducted ourselves."

Paul, together with Silvanus and Timothy, writes to the church in Thessalonica, which was young. Some doubted their motives, so he reminds them of their hard work, their affection, and their clean lives among them. He calls God as a witness because God knows even what people do not see.

For today: whoever teaches or leads others should live what they preach, both in public and in private. Ask yourself whether the way you live at home, at work, and in the church would make the gospel believable to those who watch you.
exp.0:8:
They report how Paul and his companions were received in Thessalonica. They also tell how the Thessalonians left their idols and turned to God. The "entering in" refers to the arrival or first visit. The "turned" means they changed direction, turned around. Now they serve the living and true God, in contrast to idols, which have no life.

Paul writes, together with Silvanus and Timothy, to a young church in Thessalonica. He commends them because their faith had become well known in Macedonia and Achaia. Their change was so visible that others spoke of it without Paul having to say anything. Since nearly all of them had come out of paganism, leaving their idols was a costly decision.

Today idols can be money, success, or the approval of others. Ask yourself what thing has taken the place of God in your life, and give it over to Him today. Your change, even if it is simple, can encourage others.
exp.2:5:
Paul says that Timothy has just returned from Thessalonica with good news. He tells them that the believers there remain firm in their faith and in their love. He also says that they always think of Paul and his companions with affection, and that they long to see them, just as Paul longs to see them.

Paul writes together with Silas and Timothy. He had been worried because the Thessalonians were suffering persecution, and he feared that the tempter might have caused them to fall. For this reason he sent Timothy to visit them. Timothy's report lifted a great burden from him and gave him encouragement.

Today we can encourage others in concrete ways. If you know of a brother or sister going through trials, call them, visit them, or write to them. And when you see that someone remains faithful, tell them how glad it makes you. A word spoken at the right time can strengthen someone who is weary.
exp.4:14:
This verse asks us to take care that no one repays evil with evil for the wrong they have received. Instead of taking revenge, we should always seek what is good, both among believers and toward all people.

Paul writes to the church in Thessalonica, a young community that faced pressure and rejection. Just before, he asked them to correct the disorderly with love, encourage the discouraged, and help the weak. Here he extends that care: also toward those who are not of the faith.

For today: when someone wrongs you, before you respond, pause and think of one good action you can take, such as answering calmly, praying for that person, or helping them with something concrete.
exp.4:11:
Paul asks the brothers and sisters to acknowledge certain people in the church, that is, to value them and respect them. They are the ones who labour among you, the ones who are over you in the Lord (those who lead or care for the community), and the ones who admonish you (those who warn with love in order to correct). "We beseech you" means "we ask you." The word "to know" in the verse means to recognize and honour these people.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, together with Silvanus and Timothy. He speaks to them about living with hope and encouraging one another. Here he moves on to order within the church. He does not say what offices these people held, so it is better not to assume specific titles.

For today: think about who serves you and cares for you spiritually in your church. Thank that person, pray for them, and receive their counsel with humility.
exp.4:2:
This verse says that when people are saying "Peace and safety," sudden destruction will fall on them. It will be like the pains of labor for a pregnant woman: they come suddenly and cannot be avoided. The word "pregnant" refers to a woman who is expecting a child, and "they shall not escape" refers to those who live self-assured, without taking God seriously.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, who had doubts about the return of Christ. He reminds them that the day of the Lord will come unexpectedly, like a thief in the night. Christians, by contrast, are "children of light" and can live prepared, without fear.

For today: do not place your trust only in your stability, your money, or your health. Live each day alert, with faith, honesty, and love, ready to meet the Lord.
exp.0:2:
Paul says that, when he prays to God, he does not stop remembering three things about the Thessalonians: their faith that shows itself in work, their love that shows itself in effort, and their hope that remains firm. Patience, or endurance, here means steadiness in the middle of hardships.

Paul, Silvanus and Timothy write to a young church that was facing opposition. Before correcting or teaching anything, they begin with thanks. They recognize that the lives of these believers show that their faith is genuine. Many understand that the hope refers especially to the waiting for Christ's return, which Paul mentions later in the letter.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith shows in what we do, whether our love moves us to serve, and whether our hope keeps us steady. We can also thank God in prayer for someone whose life encourages us, and tell them so.
exp.4:24:
Paul asks the believers in Thessalonica to pray for him and his companions. "Brethren" refers to the Christians in the church, and "pray" is a gentle command: "Pray for us." It is a simple request, made with humility.

Paul writes this letter together with Silvanus and Timothy. He has just prayed for the holiness of the Thessalonians and reminded them that God is faithful. Now he asks the same for himself: that they also hold him up in prayer. Although he was an apostle, he did not consider himself self-sufficient. He depended on God and on the help of his brothers and sisters in the faith.

Today we can imitate Paul in two things: praying for those who teach and serve us, such as pastors and missionaries, and encouraging ourselves to ask for prayer without shame. This week, choose one person who serves in your church and pray for them every day. If you have a need, ask someone you trust to pray for you.
exp.3:0:
Paul tells the believers in Thessalonica that he wants to ask them something important, with both affection and firmness. They have already been taught how to live so as to please God, and now he encourages them to keep growing in that. Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy to a young church facing pressures. He had already taught them how to live, and now he urges them to advance further. The verses that follow speak of holiness, including purity in sexual matters.

For today: it is not enough to have learned what is right; we must keep growing. Choose one specific area, such as how you treat others or your habits, and ask God for help to make progress in it this week.
exp.0:7:
Paul says that the word of the Lord has sounded out from the Thessalonians, not only in Macedonia and Achaia (the northern and southern regions of Greece), but in many other places. "Spread abroad" means spread widely, and "your faith toward God has gone out" means that everyone has heard of their trust in God. For this reason, Paul does not need to add anything.

Paul writes, together with Silvanus and Timothy, to a young church that was under pressure and opposition. He wants to encourage them, recognizing that their sincere faith and their joy in the middle of trial were already a testimony known to other believers.

For today: your faith speaks louder than you imagine. Living with steadfastness and hope, even in difficulties, can encourage others and point them to Christ, without the need for great speeches.
exp.4:19:
This verse says: "Despise not prophesyings." To despise something is to treat it as if it were worth nothing. Prophesyings are messages that God gives through people to encourage, correct, or guide his people. Paul asks that we not take them lightly.

Paul writes, together with Silvanus and Timothy, to the young church in Thessalonica. He gives them brief instructions for life in community. After saying "Quench not the Spirit," he adds that everything should be examined. In this way, respect for what God says is joined with careful discernment.

For today: listen with respect and attention to the teachings and words of encouragement in your church, without mocking them or dismissing them at the outset. Then compare them with the Bible and hold on to what is good.
exp.2:6:
What it says: Paul tells the brothers in Thessalonica that, through news of their faith, he and his companions were encouraged. Here "encouragement" means cheer and relief. "Affliction and distress" refers to their hardships and suffering. Knowing that they kept believing gave them strength.

Context: Paul writes this letter worried because he had to leave Thessalonica and feared that the persecution would make them abandon the faith. He sent Timothy to find out how they were doing. Timothy returned with good news of their faith and love, and Paul expresses his relief and joy. "The tempter" refers to Satan.

For today: Your firm faith may encourage others more than you imagine. Today, write to or call someone who is going through a difficult time, and tell them how their perseverance has strengthened you.
exp.2:2:
Paul says that he sent Timothy to strengthen the Thessalonians, so that no one would be shaken or waver because of the difficulties they face. "Be moved" means that someone would let themselves be shaken or discouraged by these afflictions. And "we are appointed to this" means that believers are destined to go through suffering for following Christ; it is not something unusual or a punishment.

Paul writes, together with Silas and Timothy, to a young church that was suffering opposition. He had to leave the city soon and he worried about them. Since he could not return, he sent Timothy to encourage them. He had already warned them that tribulations would come, and so it happened.

For today: when a trial comes, do not immediately think that God has abandoned you. Remember that Jesus already warned that there would be difficulties, and seek the support of brothers and sisters in the faith who encourage you to stand firm.
exp.3:7:
This verse says that whoever disregards God's instructions about living in purity and respect is not rejecting only a human being, but God himself. "Despiseth" means to treat as worthless or to pay no attention to. God has also given us his Holy Spirit, who dwells in us to help us live in a holy way.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, a young church. He reminds them of the teachings he had already given them about holiness, especially in how they treat others and in their moral life. He makes clear that these instructions are not merely his own opinion, but come from God.

For today: when the Bible corrects us in something, such as honesty or respect toward others, let us not treat it as an optional suggestion. Let us ask the Holy Spirit for help to obey with humility and to treat well those around us.
exp.3:17:
This verse calls us to encourage and comfort one another. "Comfort" means "comfort one another," and the word "unto" is an older form of "to." "These words" refers to what Paul has just explained about the return of Christ.

The apostle Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica. Some were sad because several brothers and sisters had died, and they wondered what would happen to them. Paul answers that those who died in Christ will rise first, and that all believers will be with the Lord forever. Christians interpret the details of how and when this will happen in different ways, but the central comfort is clear.

Today, when someone is grieving, do not only offer your company; also remind them tenderly of the hope of the resurrection. Share with that person a Bible passage or a simple prayer.
exp.3:8:
Paul says there is no need to write to them about love between brothers and sisters. The phrase "brotherly love" refers to love among fellow believers. The reason is that God himself has taught them to love one another.

Paul is writing to the church in Thessalonica, a young community. He had just been speaking about living in holiness, and now he recognizes that they already practice love. He shows them confidence, although in the next verse he encourages them to keep growing in that love.

For today: even if we already love our brothers and sisters, we can love more. This week, look for a concrete way to serve or support someone in your church, such as a visit, a phone call, or practical help.
exp.1:8:
He says that Paul and his companions worked with great effort and exhaustion, night and day, so that they would not be a financial burden to anyone in Thessalonica. While they worked, they also proclaimed the gospel of God.

Paul writes to the church in Thessalonica, which he helped to found. He reminds them how he lived among them: with the tenderness of a mother and of a father. He probably did manual work (many think of tentmaking, as in Acts 18:3, though it is not stated here). He wants to show that his motive was to serve, not to gain anything for himself.

For today: serve generously and without seeking advantage. If God gives you the opportunity to help others in their faith, do it with sincere effort, without taking advantage of anyone, and let your daily work also show the love of Christ.
exp.4:6:
It says that sleeping and getting drunk are things that people normally do at night. Paul uses a simple picture: night is the time of darkness, when people disconnect and lose control. Here the words "sleep" and "drunk" are clear, but they speak of something more than sleep or wine.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, who had doubts about the return of Christ. He reminds them that they belong to the light and the day. For this reason they must live awake and self-controlled, not like those who do not wait for the Lord. Many understand "sleep" as spiritual carelessness, not as ordinary rest.

Today we can ask ourselves what things make us spiritually drowsy: constant distraction, discouragement, or excess. This week, set aside time each day to pray, read the Bible, and live with clarity and hope.
exp.1:7:
He says that Paul and his companions loved the Thessalonians so much that they wanted to give them not only the gospel but also their own lives. The word "affectionately" means they truly cared for them. "Souls" here means their whole lives, themselves. "Dear" means very much loved.

Paul, together with Silvanus and Timothy, writes to the church in Thessalonica. Some might have doubted their motives, so he reminds them that they did not seek fame or money. They were gentle, like a mother caring for her children, and they worked day and night so as not to be a burden.

For today: sharing faith is not only giving correct information. It is giving time, affection, and presence. Think of someone you would like to bring closer to God, and ask yourself how you could serve them in a concrete way this week, by listening to them, accompanying them, and helping them without expecting anything in return.
exp.4:12:
They say we should value and respect very highly those who serve and lead the church, not for their person or their position, but for the work they do. Then he adds: "be at peace among yourselves," that is, live in harmony. The word "esteem" means appreciation and respect.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, a young church that was going through pressures. Earlier he speaks of the leaders who labor, direct, and counsel. Paul knows that if that service is not valued, tensions can arise. That is why he joins respect for the leaders with peace among everyone.

Today we can thank in concrete ways those who serve in our church: a message, a prayer, or practical help. And if there is some tension with someone, we can take the first step toward peace with humility.
exp.1:10:
Paul says that the Thessalonians know well how he and his companions treated them. They exhorted them, that is, they encouraged them to live well, and they comforted them, in other words, they stood beside them in their sorrow. They did this with each one personally, as a father cares for his children. The word "burdensome" in the previous verse is explained here in a way that does not need to be quoted further.

Paul writes together with Silas and Timothy to a young church that was under pressure because of its faith. Earlier he had spoken of his tenderness as that of a mother who nurses her children. Now he adds the image of the father. He wants to remind them that his ministry was sincere, free of self-interest, and full of affection.

Today, if we guide others in faith, in the family or in the church, it is not enough simply to teach. We must draw near to each person, encourage them with patience, comfort them and set an example, as a good father would do.
exp.1:1:
Paul says that he and his companions had already suffered and been mistreated in Philippi, and yet they had the courage to speak of the gospel in Thessalonica. "Humiliated" and "treated with contempt" describe what they endured. "Boldness" is courage and daring. "Fierce conflict" can be understood as strong opposition or intense struggle.

Paul writes together with Silas and Timothy to the church in Thessalonica, which was newly formed. He recalls their arrival to show that his message was sincere and not a tactic to gain something. According to Acts 16, in Philippi they were beaten and imprisoned. That they kept preaching after that supports their honesty.

For today: when you are rejected or hurt for doing what is right, do not depend on your own strength. Paul says that his boldness came from God. Ask Him for encouragement and keep sharing, with humility and firmness, what He has entrusted to you.
exp.3:6:
This verse says that God did not call us to live in impurity, but to live set apart for him. "Impurity" means uncleanness, especially in sexual conduct. "Holiness" means being set apart for God and living in a clean and faithful way. "Called" refers to God's invitation to follow him.

Paul is writing to believers in Thessalonica, a young church surrounded by a pagan culture. Before this verse, he asks them not to live with uncontrolled desires or take advantage of others, and to care for their brothers and sisters. Afterward, he reminds them that rejecting this teaching means rejecting God, who gave them his Holy Spirit.

For today: before deciding what to watch, say, or do, ask yourself whether it honors God and respects others. Ask the Holy Spirit to help you live with purity and respect.
exp.3:16:
It says that when Christ returns, the Christians who are still alive will be caught up suddenly, carried away together with those who have already died in Christ. They will meet the Lord in the air, and from then on they will be with Him forever. "Á" is the old form of "a", and "juntamente" means "at the same time".

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, who were sad and confused about the brothers and sisters who had died. They feared that those who had died would miss the coming of Christ. Paul comforts them: those who have died in Christ will rise first. Christians differ in how they understand the timing and details of this being "caught up", but all of them share the central hope.

When you feel grief for someone who died in Christ, or fear about the future, remember this promise. Comfort others with it, as Paul asks in the next verse.
exp.4:5:
This verse invites us not to live distracted or indifferent, like those who are asleep. To be alert means to stay attentive and awake. To be clear-headed means to think with clarity and live with self-control. Those who do not know Christ or wait for his return are the ones the verse sets apart from believers.

Paul writes to the Christians of Thessalonica, a young church that had doubts about the return of Jesus. He reminds them that they are children of the light, so that day should not catch them by surprise like a thief. For this reason he encourages them to live with attention and steadfastness, protected by faith, love, and hope.

Today we can apply this by caring for everyday life: setting aside a few minutes each day to pray and read the Bible, and avoiding whatever dulls us spiritually, such as too many screens or excessive worries. In this way we live ready and full of hope.
exp.0:5:
The explanation says that the believers in Thessalonica followed the example of Paul and his companions, and in this way also the example of the Lord Jesus. They received the message of the gospel even though it cost them much suffering, yet they did so with the joy that the Holy Ghost gives. "Affliction" means distress, pressure, or persecution. "Followers" are those who follow an example.

Paul writes, together with Silas and Timothy, to a young church that had been born in the midst of opposition (Acts 17). He commends them because their faith was real, not just words. Their way of living and of enduring suffering became an example for other churches in the region.

Today, Christian joy does not depend on everything going well. When obeying God costs you something, ask the Holy Spirit for his joy and trust that your steadfastness can encourage others.
exp.4:17:
He says we should give thanks "in every thing," that is, in every circumstance, not necessarily "for every thing." The phrase "for you" means "for you," addressed to you. Giving thanks is something God desires from those who belong to Christ.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, a young church facing pressure and suffering. This verse is part of a series of brief exhortations: joy, constant prayer, and gratitude. Together they show how to live in fellowship with God day by day. Paul does not say that everything that happens is good, but that God remains worthy of thanks in the midst of everything.

Today, you can begin or end your day by naming aloud three specific things for which you give thanks to God. Do this also on difficult days: thank him for his companionship, his care, and the small blessings that are still present.
exp.4:15:
This verse invites us to live with joy in a steady way. The word "Rejoice" calls for a joy that continues, and the word "evermore" shows that joy should not depend only on the good moments.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, a young church that faced opposition. Just before this, he asks them to look after one another, with patience and without repaying evil with evil. Just after, he speaks of praying without ceasing and giving thanks in everything. This joy is not simply good humor, but a joy that springs from the relationship with Christ.

For today: when a difficult day comes, pause for a moment and name one good thing God has given you, such as his care, your family, or his forgiveness. Giving thanks for it quietly can help you remember that your joy rests in God, not in circumstances.
exp.2:0:
This verse says that Paul and his companions could no longer bear the worry about the believers in Thessalonica. So they decided to be left alone in Athens. The phrase "could no longer bear" means they could no longer endure the anguish of not knowing how those believers were doing. "We thought it good" means they made the decision together.

The speaker is Paul, together with Silas and Timothy, as the opening of the letter shows. They had left Thessalonica because of opposition, and the new believers were facing pressure. Paul, in Athens, chose to be without companionship so that Timothy could be sent to learn how their faith was holding up. It shows real pastoral affection.

For today: when you worry about someone in the faith, do not carry that concern alone. Pray for that person, seek them out, write to them, or walk alongside them. A simple act of care can strengthen them a great deal.
exp.0:6:
It says that the believers in Thessalonica became a model to follow for all the other believers in Macedonia and Achaia. The word "ensamples" means a pattern or example that others can imitate. "Achaia" was the region of southern Greece, and "Macedonia" the northern region, where Thessalonica was located.

Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy to a young church that had received the gospel in the midst of suffering. Before this verse, he reminds them that they imitated the apostles and the Lord, and that they received the word with joy despite the tribulation. Their faith did not go unnoticed, and others saw it.

For today: our faith is always being observed by someone, even when we do not notice it. When we persevere with joy in difficult times, we encourage others to trust God. Ask yourself today: what will others see in my way of believing and living?
exp.4:3:
Paul tells the believers in Thessalonica that they do not live in darkness, that is, in spiritual ignorance or far from God. That is why the day of the Lord will not catch them by surprise, like a thief who comes without warning. The word "overtake" means that it would reach them suddenly and find them unprepared.

Paul writes to a young church that had doubts about the coming of the Lord. He has just said that for those who live secure, saying "peace and safety," that day will arrive all at once. Here he contrasts them with the believers, who belong to the light and must live awake.

For today: there is no need to live in fear of the future, but there is a need to live with attention. We can set aside a moment each day to pray, read the Bible, and examine our lives, so that we are ready and at peace with God.
exp.1:14:
The verse says that some of the people who were in Judea at that time rejected God by their actions: they killed Jesus and the prophets, they persecuted Paul and his companions, they do not please God, and they oppose all people.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, who were suffering persecution from their own countrymen. He compares them with the churches in Judea, which suffered the same things.

Paul was Jewish and loved his people (Romans 9:1-3). Here he speaks of certain specific opponents, not of all Jews, since Jesus, the apostles, and many early believers were Jewish. Some scholars believe he uses strong language, as the ancient prophets did.

When you suffer rejection for your faith, do not be surprised or become bitter. Other believers have gone through the same thing. Stand firm, take encouragement from the fellowship of your church, and never use this text to look down on any people.
exp.2:12:
Paul asks that God strengthen and establish the inner life of believers, so that their lives will be holy and blameless before God, our Father. This will be evident when Jesus returns "with all his saints." "Blameless" means without any ground for reproach. "Established" means strengthened, made firm.

Paul writes, together with Silvanus and Timothy, to the young church in Thessalonica, which was under pressure and persecution. He has just prayed that their love would grow, and now he says that this love helps them have a firm heart. "His saints" may refer to believers, to angels, or to both; interpreters understand it in different ways.

For today: do not rely only on your own effort to be faithful. Ask God every day for a steadfast heart, and practice concrete love toward those around you, remembering that Christ will return.
exp.4:8:
This verse says that God did not appoint us to his wrath, that is, to final punishment, but to receive salvation through Jesus Christ.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, who were waiting for Christ's return and had doubts about the future. Earlier he called them children of the day and asked them to live alert, self-controlled, and protected by faith, love, and the hope of salvation. This verse gives them the reason for their confidence: their future depends on what Christ has done for them.

For today: when you feel fear about the future or guilt over your failures, remember that your security rests in Christ, not in your performance. That hope encourages you to live with courage, attentiveness, and love toward others.
exp.1:19:
They say the believers in Thessalonica are Paul's and his companions' glory and joy. Glory means a source of pride and honor; joy is deep gladness. Paul does not speak of his own achievements, but of the people who believed in Christ.

Paul writes to the church in Thessalonica. He had had to leave the city because of opposition, and he wanted to return, but he says that Satan hindered us. He does not explain how; there are several possibilities, and it is not wise to insist on just one. Even so, his love for them remains firm, and he sees them as his crown before Jesus at his coming.

For today: value the people God has placed in your path, especially those who believe with you. Encourage them, pray for them, and give them your time. What we leave behind that matters most is not things, but lives that grow in Christ.
exp.1:12:
Paul gives thanks to God without ceasing because the Thessalonians heard the message and did not treat it as a simple human opinion. They received it for what it truly is: the word of God. And that word continues to work with power in them, the ones who believed.

Paul, together with Silvanus and Timothy, writes to a young church in Thessalonica. He reminds them of how he cared for them like a father. Now he rejoices that they accepted the gospel with faith, even in the middle of the opposition he mentions next.

For today: when you read the Bible, do not open it only to look for interesting ideas. Read it with humility, asking God to use it to change you, and let it work on the way you think and live.
exp.1:17:
Paul says that he wanted to visit the Thessalonians, and not just once but "once and again." But "Satan hindered us," that is, Satan got in the way and put an obstacle in the path that prevented the journey. The word "hindered" here means that the way was blocked.

Paul writes to the church in Thessalonica, which he had founded not long before. He had to leave the city because of persecution, and now he was far away. He wants them to know that he did not abandon them out of lack of affection. The text does not explain how Satan acted; some think of opposition from enemies, and others of difficult circumstances.

For today: when something hinders you from doing a good you desire, do not conclude that your love was false or that God has left you. Keep loving, keep praying, and look for other ways to serve, as Paul did when he wrote this letter.
exp.1:13:
Paul tells the believers in Thessalonica that they have become like the Christian churches in Judea. "Followers" does not mean they copied them on purpose, but that they went through the same thing: they suffered mistreatment from their own countrymen, just as the believers in Judea suffered it from other Jews.

Paul, together with Silas and Timothy, writes to a young church that faced rejection because of its faith. He wants to encourage it: what they are living through is not a sign that something has gone wrong, but something other believers have also gone through. They received the message as the word of God, and that is why they persevere.

For today: if you face mockery or rejection for following Christ, do not lose heart or feel alone. Remember that brothers and sisters around the world go through something similar, and seek encouragement from them in the church.
exp.4:13:
This verse calls the whole church to look after one another. Paul urges them to admonish, that is, to correct with kindness, those who live in an unruly way: those who are not carrying out their responsibilities. They are to comfort the fainthearted, the discouraged or fearful. They are to support the weak, those who are frail, probably in faith or in strength. And they are to be patient with everyone.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, a young church facing pressure and doubt. Just before this verse he speaks about respect for their leaders. Here the care extends to all the brothers and sisters. Some understand that the unruly are those who had stopped working, since the letter mentions this earlier, though the term is broad.

Today, before reacting to someone who falls short or is weak, ask yourself what they need: correction, encouragement or support? And walk alongside them with patience.
exp.4:26:
He says that Paul gives a very serious charge that this letter be read to all the believers. The word "I charge you" in the verse above stands for a solemn request made with authority, as one who puts someone under oath before God. "Holy" does not refer to people who are perfect, but to those who belong to God.

The apostle Paul is speaking near the end of his first letter to the church in Thessalonica. Up to this point he has encouraged those believers to live with faith, hope, and love. He may have wanted to make sure no one was left out, since letters were read aloud in the gatherings. Some think there were tensions in the church, but the text does not say so clearly. The closing note about Athens was added later and is not part of the original text.

For today: God wants his Word to reach everyone. Try to read it and share it with your family and your church, leaving no one out.
exp.3:1:
This verse reminds the Thessalonians that they already know the instructions that Paul and his companions gave them. "Commandments" here means instructions or teachings with authority. And "by the Lord Jesus" means that these instructions had the backing of Christ himself, and were not simply human opinions.

Paul, together with Silvanus and Timothy, writes to a young church that had received teaching not long before. He is not presenting something new, but encouraging them to keep growing in what they have already learned. Right away he speaks of sanctification and of purity in sexual life, a very needed topic in a city with pagan customs.

For today: it is not enough to know what God teaches; we must practice it. Think of one biblical teaching you already know well and ask God for help to live it out this week.
exp.4:7:
They say that believers, who belong to the day (to the light), must live with soberness, that is, with a clear and watchful mind and self-control. Paul uses the image of a soldier: faith and love are the breastplate that protects the chest, and the hope of salvation is the helmet that protects the head.

Paul writes to the Christians of Thessalonica, a young church that faced pressure and doubts about the return of Christ. He has just contrasted the night, with its sleep and drunkenness, with the day. He reminds them that God did not appoint them to wrath, but to salvation through Jesus.

For today: when anxiety or temptation comes, guard your heart and your mind on purpose. Trust God, love the people near you, and remember that your future is secure in Christ.
exp.1:4:
Paul says that he and his companions never used words of flattery, that is, false praise meant to win people over. Nor did they act out of greed, which is a desire for money or gain. The Thessalonians know this because they saw it for themselves, and God himself is witness to what is in the heart.

Paul, together with Silvanus and Timothy, writes to the church in Thessalonica. Some may have questioned their motives, so he reminds them how they proclaimed the gospel. They did not seek to please people, but God, who examines the hearts. Their conduct was open and sincere, without hidden agendas.

For today: before you speak about God or help someone, examine your motives. Ask yourself whether you are seeking approval, benefit, or recognition. Ask God to give you a sincere heart, and speak with truth and love, without manipulating anyone.
exp.1:16:
Paul says that he and his companions were separated from the Thessalonians only for a short time. They were away "in presence," that is, physically, but not "in heart," because they remained united in affection. For this reason, all the more eagerly, they made every effort ("endeavoured the more abundantly") to see their faces again with "great desire," a deep longing.

Paul writes to a young church that had been left behind in the middle of opposition and persecution. He had been forced to leave there, and he feared they might think he had abandoned them. With these words he shows them that his affection remains firm and that he has not forgotten them.

Today, distance does not have to cool love. Think of a brother, sister, or family member you have not seen in a long time, and look for them this week with a phone call, a message, or a visit. In this way you show them that they still have a place in your heart.
exp.1:0:
Paul reminds the brothers in Thessalonica that they themselves know that his arrival in the city was not "vain," that is, it was not empty, useless, or without fruit. Paul appeals to what they saw and experienced with him.

Paul writes together with Silas and Timothy. This letter is addressed to a young church that had only recently come to know the gospel. Some may have questioned the intentions of the missionaries, so Paul reminds them how they came: with courage, even after suffering and being mistreated in Philippi, and with a sincere message.

A life that is consistent and sincere gives weight to what we say about God. Today we can ask ourselves whether our words of faith are backed up by how we treat others day to day, even when it is costly.
exp.2:1:
Paul says that he sent Timothy to visit the believers in Thessalonica. He calls him "brother," "servant of God" (someone who serves God), and "fellow worker" in the gospel. His task was to strengthen and to encourage and counsel the Thessalonians in their faith.

Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy. They had been forced to leave Thessalonica because of opposition, and Paul, worried about the young church, could bear it no longer without news. He stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy. He wanted the believers not to lose heart because of the trials they were suffering.

Today we can imitate this care: when someone in your church or family goes through difficulties, do not leave them alone. A visit, a phone call, or a word of encouragement based on the Bible can strengthen their faith more than you imagine.
exp.3:4:
It says that each one should take care of his own intimate life without letting himself be carried away by disordered desire. "Lust of concupiscence" refers to an uncontrolled passion or craving, especially sexual. "Gentiles" are the peoples who were not Jews and who, in this case, did not know the true God. Paul says that believers must not live as they do.

Paul writes to the Christians of Thessalonica, a young church made up of people who came from paganism. He wants to encourage them to live differently, because God called them to holiness. Some understand "his vessel" as the body itself, and others as the wife; the text allows both readings.

For today: before acting on impulse, ask yourself whether you know God in that decision. Ask him for help to master your desires, to care for your relationships, and to treat others with respect and purity.
exp.4:18:
It says we should not "quench" the Spirit, as one puts out a fire or a flame. The word "quench" is the same idea used for putting out a lamp or a bonfire. That is, we should not cool, smother, or stop what the Holy Spirit wants to do in us and among us.

The apostle Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, a young church facing pressure. At the end of the letter he gives brief advice about life in community. This command goes together with care for prophecies: do not despise them, but test everything. Scholars explain in several ways how the Spirit could be "quenched," for example through contempt, disorder, or resistance.

For today: when you feel the urge to pray, forgive, or help someone, do not ignore it out of fear or laziness. Obey it, and always confirm that it agrees with the Bible.
exp.2:10:
Paul asks that God himself, our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ, direct his way to you, that is, that they open the road and guide him so that he can reach the Thessalonians.

Paul, together with Silvanus and Timothy, writes to the church in Thessalonica, whom he had to leave soon and with sorrow. He tells them that he prays night and day to see them again and to help them grow in faith. He recognizes that it does not depend on him, but on God, that the way be opened. In chapter 2 he mentions that Satan blocked their path.

For today: when you make plans, bring your ways before God and ask Him to direct them. You may plan with effort, but with humility, trusting that He opens and closes doors according to His good will.
exp.0:1:
Paul says that he and his companions always give thanks to God for all the believers in Thessalonica. They remember them by name in their prayers. The word "you all" in the verse refers to everyone in the congregation, and the phrase "making mention of you" means "remembering you" or "bringing you up" in prayer.

The speakers are Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, who are writing to a young church in Thessalonica. Paul had founded it not long before, in the midst of opposition. Before correcting or teaching anything, he begins by acknowledging what God was doing among them. Notice that he gives thanks for "all of you," leaving no one out.

Today we can imitate this habit. Think of your family, your church, or your companions, and before asking God for something on their behalf, give thanks for something good you see in their lives. Say it in prayer, and if you can, tell them as well.
exp.3:15:
This verse says that the Lord Jesus himself will come down from heaven with a loud command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God. When that happens, the believers who have already died will rise first. "Shout" is a loud voice of command, and "sleep" is a gentle way of speaking about the death of believers.

Paul writes to the Christians of Thessalonica, who were sad and confused about their loved ones who had died. They feared that those who had died would miss the return of Christ. Paul explains to them that this is not so: those who died in Christ will not be left behind, but will rise first. Scholars understand the details of these events in different ways, but the comfort is clear.

For today: if you have lost someone who believed in Jesus, you can grieve with hope. Death does not have the last word. Comfort others with these words, as Paul asks.
exp.4:27:
He says that Paul wishes the grace of Jesus Christ, his undeserved favor and help, to be with all the believers in Thessalonica. The word "Amen" is a way of saying "so be it."

The closing note, which says the letter was written from Athens, is not part of what Paul wrote. It is a note that later copyists added to some manuscripts. Also, many scholars believe the letter was written from Corinth, though others debate this.

Paul closes his letter to a young church that was under pressure and had doubts about the return of Christ. He has just asked that the letter be read to everyone, without leaving anyone out. He ends with a blessing, as he does in almost all of his letters, reminding them that everything they live depends on Christ.

Today we can end the day, a difficult conversation, or a meeting by asking for the grace of Christ for others. It is a simple way to remember that we do not move forward by our own strength, but by his favor.
exp.4:20:
It says we should test, examine, and put to the proof all things, and keep hold only of what is good.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, a young church. Just before this, he asks them not to put out the Spirit or despise prophecies, that is, the messages given within the congregation. But he does not ask them to believe everything without thinking: those messages were to be evaluated. Then he tells them to stay away from every kind of evil. Scholars understand the testing in several ways, but the context points to teachings and spiritual messages.

Today, before accepting a sermon, a video, or spiritual advice, compare it with what the Bible teaches, pray for wisdom, and hold on to whatever is true and builds up faith.
exp.1:6:
This verse says that Paul and his companions were gentle and kind toward the believers in Thessalonica, like a mother who nurses her children and cares for them with affection. The word "gentle" means mild or tender, and the phrase about the mother means that she tenderly holds and looks after them. Some versions translate "gentle" as "children," since the ancient manuscripts vary at this point.

Paul, together with Silas and Timothy, writes to a young church. He has just said that they did not act with flattering words or with greed for money or fame, even though as apostles they had the right to ask for support. Now he describes their manner toward them with tenderness, and then says that they loved them so much that they would give them even their own lives.

For today: when you teach or correct others, do it with patience and affection, not with harshness or out of pride. Truth is received best when it comes with sincere love and real care.
exp.4:25:
Paul asks the Thessalonians to greet all the brothers and sisters with a holy kiss. The word "kiss" here is the English word the verse uses, and it was a common greeting in that day. It is called "holy" because it expresses a clean and pure affection between believers.

Paul writes at the end of his letter, as he is saying goodbye. He had encouraged them, corrected them, and taught them. In that time, a kiss on the cheek was a common greeting among family members and friends. Paul takes this as a sign that the church is a family. He says "all," so no one is left out. Some believe the instruction was meant for the whole church gathered together; the text gives no further details.

Today the custom matters less than the spirit behind it: welcoming everyone with sincere warmth. You can greet people with a hug, a handshake, or a kind word, especially reaching out to someone who often ends up alone or overlooked.
exp.2:9:
Paul says that he prays night and day, with great earnestness, that he may see the Thessalonians again face to face. He also wants to "perfect that which is lacking in your faith," that is, to complete or strengthen what they still need in their Christian life. "Earnestness" here means urgent, persistent insistence, and his prayer is very intense and constant.

Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy to a young church that had to be left quickly because of persecution. Timothy brought him good news that they remained firm, and this filled him with joy. Even so, Paul knows that their faith still needs to keep growing, and he desires to teach them more in person.

For today: faith is strengthened in community. Pray steadily for someone in your church, and look for a concrete way to encourage or teach them something this week.
exp.4:1:
Paul reminds the believers in Thessalonica of something they already know well: the "day of the Lord," that is, the moment when God will intervene decisively, will come by surprise, like a thief in the night. "You know" is what the phrase means here, and the coming is something certain, even though no one knows when it will happen.

Paul writes to a young church that had doubts about the return of Christ. He tells them they do not need dates or calendars, because they already know what is essential. Then he contrasts those who say "peace and security" with believers, who do not live in darkness, meaning they are not caught unprepared.

For today: instead of worrying about guessing dates, let us live each day with faith, honesty, and love, like people who are ready. If Christ is your confidence, his coming is not a threat but a hope.
exp.4:16:
This verse invites us to pray continually. "Without ceasing" means without stopping, never letting up. It does not mean always being on our knees with our eyes closed, but living with our hearts turned toward God at every moment. The Greek word used here was also used for a persistent cough that comes and goes, meaning something constant and repeated.

Paul writes this letter to the church in Thessalonica, a young community facing pressures. At the end of the letter he gives brief, practical advice for Christian living. This command comes between "rejoice always" and "give thanks in everything," so prayer appears joined to joy and gratitude.

Today you can offer short prayers throughout the day: when you wake up, on the way somewhere, before a decision, or in the middle of a difficulty. A simple phrase like "Lord, help me" or "Thank you, God" is already speaking with Him.
exp.3:10:
This verse asks believers for three simple things: to work at living quietly, to attend to their own affairs, and to work with their own hands.

Paul, together with Silvanus and Timothy, writes to the church in Thessalonica. He has just praised their love for one another and encourages them to grow even more. Then he reminds them of what he had already taught them. Some think certain believers were neglecting their work, but the text does not say so with certainty. Paul explains that in this way their witness would be honest before outsiders.

For today: fulfill your work and your duties faithfully, without getting involved in gossip or other people's conflicts. A quiet and responsible life can be a good witness to those who observe you.
exp.4:22:
Paul prays that God, whom he calls the God of peace, would make them holy completely, that is, in every way. To make holy means to set apart for God and make holy. The word "blameless" here means faultless, with nothing to be held against them. He asks that their spirit, soul, and body be kept whole and without blemish until the coming of Jesus Christ.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, a young church facing pressure and doubts about the return of Christ. After giving practical advice, such as testing everything and staying away from evil, he makes clear that holiness does not depend only on their own effort. The verses that follow confirm this: God is faithful, and he will do it. Some debate whether "spirit, soul, and body" describes three distinct parts or simply the whole person.

Today, instead of living your faith halfway, give God your whole life: your thoughts, emotions, and daily habits. And ask him, with confidence, to sustain you.
exp.1:2:
Paul says that his message did not come from error or false ideas. It also did not come from dirty or impure motives, nor did he intend to deceive anyone. "Exhortation" refers to the preaching and encouragement they gave. "Uncleanness" speaks of impurity, that is, twisted intentions. "Deceit" means using tricks to get some benefit.

Paul, together with Silas and Timothy, writes to the believers in Thessalonica. They had just been mistreated in Philippi, and yet they preached with courage. It seems some were doubting their motives, and so he reminds them how they behaved among them, with honesty and without seeking gain.

For today: before you share or teach anything about God, examine your motives. Ask yourself whether you are seeking applause or personal benefit, or whether you truly want to serve God and help others with the truth.
exp.1:15:
Paul says that some of his opponents were hindering him from preaching to the Gentiles (non-Jews) so that they might be saved. By this, the phrase "to fill up their sins" means to bring their account of sin to the very brim. The words "to the uttermost" indicate that God's judgment was coming upon them completely or finally.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, who were suffering opposition from their own countrymen, just as the churches of Judea were. He speaks with grief, not with hatred: he himself was a Jew. He does not accuse the whole Jewish people, but those who killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets and who persecuted them. Some understand "the wrath" as a judgment already seen, others as one still to come; the text does not make this entirely clear.

Today, do not use faith to look down on anyone. If someone opposes the gospel, pray for that person and keep sharing the message with love and firmness.
exp.4:9:
This verse says that Jesus Christ died for us. His death has a purpose: that we should live together with him, whether we are awake and alive or asleep, a biblical way of speaking of those who have already died. The word "together" means "in company with, united."

Paul writes to the Christians of Thessalonica, who were anxious about the return of Christ and about the believers who had already died. Earlier he told them that God did not appoint them to wrath, but to salvation. This verse closes that idea with a promise: neither life nor death separates us from Christ. Then he asks them to encourage one another with these words.

For today: when you feel fear about the future or about death, remember that your security rests on what Christ has already done. Use it to comfort someone this week.
exp.3:9:
Paul tells the Thessalonians that they already practice love toward all the believers in Macedonia, the region where Thessalonica was. Even so, he asks them to increase more and more, that is, to grow even further in that love. The word "but" in the verse marks the turn from praise to request, and "brotherly love" is the love among brothers and sisters in the faith.

Paul writes, together with his companions, to a young church that was under pressure. Before correcting them, he acknowledges them: their love was already real and well known. Then he encourages them not to settle, since Christian love can always grow. After that he gives practical advice about living quietly and working with honesty.

For today: even if you already love your church, ask God whom you can serve better this week. It might be a phone call, a visit, or a concrete act of help. Love grows when it is practiced.
exp.4:4:
Paul says that all the believers in Thessalonica are children of light and children of the day. The phrase "children of" was a way of saying that someone belongs to something and identifies with it. The archaic words "é" and "vosotros" mean "and" and "you all," so they are dropped from this rendering. Paul adds that we do not belong to the night or to darkness.

Paul is writing to a young church that had questions about the return of Christ. Earlier he spoke of people who will say "peace and safety" and will be caught off guard by judgment. Here he encourages the believers: they do not live in darkness, so that day has no reason to take them by surprise. Then he calls them to stay alert and sober.

For today: ask yourself whether the way you live, speak, and make decisions shows that you belong to the light. Today, set aside one hidden or doubtful action and practice something clear and honest, trusting that God has made you his own.
exp.4:23:
He says God is faithful, that is, trustworthy and constant in what he promises. He is the one who called us to be his, and so he will also bring to completion what he began. "Will do it" refers to what was said before: to sanctify us completely and to keep us blameless until the coming of Jesus Christ. The words "you" and "who" in the older wording of this verse are the same as the forms we use today.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, a young church facing pressure and doubts about the return of Christ. He has just prayed that God would sanctify them in their whole being. This verse closes that prayer with assurance: the work does not depend only on their own effort, but on the faithfulness of God.

For today: when you feel weak or tired in your faith, rest in the fact that God does not abandon what he began in you. Pray with confidence and keep obeying him step by step, knowing that he sustains you.
exp.1:5:
Paul says that neither he nor his companions sought to be praised by people, not from the Thessalonians or from anyone else. Although as apostles of Christ they could have demanded respect or support, and could have been a burden to others, especially financially, they chose not to do so.

Paul writes together with Silas and Timothy to a young church. Some doubted their motives, and he reminds them that they did not speak with flattery or for money. Their aim was to please God, who examines the heart. This shows in how they treated them with tenderness, like a mother caring for her children.

Today we can examine why we serve: are we looking for applause or recognition, or do we want to please God and bless others? Before we serve or speak about the faith, let us ask God to purify our intentions and give us sincere love for people.
exp.3:13:
It says that our faith rests on a fact: Jesus died and rose again. For this reason, God will also bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in him. "Fallen asleep" is a gentle way of saying that they died, and the small word for "to" is the old way of writing it. The idea is that the death of believers is not the end: God will bring them with Christ.

Paul writes to the Christians in Thessalonica, who were sad and confused about fellow believers who had died. He wanted them not to grieve like people who have no hope. So he bases his comfort on the resurrection of Jesus. The details of how and when everything will happen are explained in different ways among Christians.

For today: when the pain comes over the death of someone loved in Christ, you may truly weep and at the same time rest in God's promise. Comfort others with this hope, with simple words and with your presence.
exp.1:3:
Paul says that God examined them and approved them, and for that reason entrusted them with the gospel. Therefore they speak as people who want to please God, not other people. Being approved means they passed a test. Trying to please people means seeking to be liked by others. And God "tests our hearts," that is, he looks closely at our deepest intentions.

Paul writes together with Silas and Timothy to the believers in Thessalonica. They had just been mistreated in Philippi, yet they proclaimed the message with boldness anyway. Some were questioning them, so Paul defends that his message and his motives were sincere, without deceit or any desire for gain.

For today: before you speak about your faith or serve others, ask yourself whom you want to please. Ask God to examine your heart and give you the courage to be sincere, even when you are not always applauded.
exp.3:5:
This verse says that no one should take advantage of their brother or deceive him in anything. "Oppress" here means going too far, taking advantage. "Avenger" means that God executes justice, and "protested" means warned with great seriousness. Paul reminds them that he had already given them this warning.

The one speaking is Paul, together with Silas and Timothy, writing to the believers in Thessalonica. They came from a pagan culture where immorality was common. Many understand that the verse continues the theme of sexuality, that is, not harming a brother by seducing his wife or abusing him. Others see it as a broader warning against any kind of fraud. The text allows both readings.

For today: treat others with honesty and respect in your relationships, your work, and your business. Before deciding something, ask yourself whether it would harm or deceive someone, remembering that God sees and brings justice.
exp.1:11:
It says that Paul, Silas, and Timothy urged the believers in Thessalonica to live in a way that honors God. The phrase "urged" here means earnestly pleading with them and solemnly testifying to them. The reason is that God called them into his kingdom and glory, that is, into sharing his rule and his presence.

Paul reminds them how he behaved toward them: with holiness, righteousness, and without fault, like a father who encourages and comforts his children. He wants them to see that his advice came from sincere care, not from self-interest. Then he gives thanks that they received the message as the word of God, even in the midst of suffering.

For today: if God has called you to something so great, your daily life can reflect it. Today, choose one concrete decision, at home or at work, and carry it out with honesty and love, as someone who belongs to God.
exp.4:0:
Paul tells the brothers and sisters in Thessalonica that there is no need for him to write to them about the times and the seasons. The word "but" at the start of the verse is simply the ordinary word "but," and "times and seasons" refers to the dates and periods when the final events will happen, such as the coming of the Lord.

Paul writes this letter to a young church that had questions about Christ's return (he had already spoken about it in 4:13-18). He reminds them that they already know the essentials: the day of the Lord will arrive unexpectedly, like a thief in the night. That is why they do not need calendars, but need to stay ready. Jesus himself said that no one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36).

Today we can set aside our curiosity about dates and live each day with faith, love, and faithfulness, ready to meet the Lord whenever He chooses.
exp.0:4:
Paul says that the gospel did not come to the Thessalonians in words alone, but also in power, with the Holy Spirit and with full conviction. The word "power" means strength or force, and "much assurance" is understood as great confidence or certainty. They also saw how Paul and his companions lived among them, with sincere love.

Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy to the church of Thessalonica, which was young and under pressure. He reminds them that their faith is real, because God was at work among them and they saw a life that matched the message. This encouraged them to remain firm, imitating Christ in the midst of tribulation.

Today, it is not enough to talk about Jesus; it also matters to live with love and to depend on the Spirit. This week, try to make the way you treat someone speak of the gospel as much as your words do.
exp.3:2:
This verse says that God wants us to be holy, that is, to live set apart for Him. And it gives a concrete example: that we keep away from sexual immorality, which means any sexual relationship outside of marriage. The phrase "that ye should abstain" means to keep yourselves far away from it, not merely to avoid falling into it.

The one speaking is Paul, together with Silvanus and Timothy, writing to the believers in Thessalonica. They were new Christians, surrounded by a pagan culture that saw sex outside of marriage as something normal. Paul reminds them of what he had already taught them and encourages them to keep growing so as to please God.

For today: holiness includes the way we care for our bodies and our relationships. Today you can decide which things, places, or content lead you into temptation, and stay away from them with the help of God and trustworthy brothers and sisters.
exp.0:9:
It says that the believers of Thessalonica wait for Jesus, the Son of God, to come from heaven. God raised him from the dead. Jesus delivered us from the wrath to come. The word "á" is an old way of spelling "a," and "libró" means rescued or saved.

Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy to the newly formed church in Thessalonica. He reminds them that their faith is famous throughout the region: they turned away from idols to serve the living God, and now they wait for Jesus. The "wrath to come" is understood as God's judgment on sin. Christians differ in how they understand the timing and the details of that judgment.

For today: live with a settled hope. If Jesus has already rescued you, you do not need to live in fear of the future. May that hope help you serve God with joy and be faithful in everyday life while you wait for his return.

sum.2: Paul, worried about the Thessalonians, sent Timothy to strengthen their faith in the middle of their trials. Timothy came back with good news about their faith and love. Paul was filled with joy and thankfulness, and he prayed that he would be able to visit them, and that their love would grow and their hearts would stay holy until the coming of Christ.
sum.4: Paul reminds them that the day of the Lord will arrive suddenly, like a thief in the night, but believers, as children of the light, must stay alert, self-controlled, and confident in the salvation that comes through Christ. He asks them to respect their leaders, help one another, do good, always be joyful, pray without ceasing, and give thanks. He closes by trusting that God is faithful.
sum.0: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy thank God for the believers in Thessalonica, remembering their active faith, their hardworking love, and their steadfast hope in Jesus. They received the gospel with joy even though they were suffering, and their example became known in many places. They turned away from idols to serve the living God and to wait for Jesus, who rescues them from the coming wrath.
sum.1: Paul reminds the Thessalonians that he preached the gospel to them with courage and honesty, without seeking fame or money. He treated them with the gentleness of a mother and the care of a father, and he worked day and night so that he would not be a burden to them. They received the message as the word of God, they suffered persecution, and Paul longs to see them again.
sum.3: Paul encourages the Thessalonians to keep growing in a life that pleases God: living in holiness, with purity, without taking advantage of anyone, loving one another, and working with honesty. He also comforts them by saying that believers who have died in Jesus will rise first, and then those who are still alive will meet the Lord, so that they will be with Him forever.
